insight.title: T. Rex Lived Closer to Humans Than Stegosaurus
insight.subtitle: Stegosaurus was already an ancient fossil long before T. Rex ever walked the Earth.
insight.notificationHook: T. Rex is closer to us than Stegosaurus

sections.text: Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago, while T. Rex appeared 66 million years ago. That means T. Rex is chronologically closer to the invention of the iPhone than to a live Stegosaurus.
Movies lump all dinosaurs into one big prehistoric family reunion, but their era lasted so long that these two iconic species were separated by over eighty million years of quiet evolution.
If a T. Rex went to a museum during its own era, a Stegosaurus exhibit would already qualify as ancient history—complete with millions of years of accumulated dust.
Pop culture made them roommates, but time made them strangers.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is everything that matters today.

First up, the United States Federal Reserve has decided to keep interest rates steady for now, citing elevated inflation that refuses to cool down. For you, this means borrowing costs on everything from mortgages to credit cards will stay high, as central banks continue struggling to balance economic growth with rising prices.

Meanwhile, lawmakers in the U.S. Senate are fast-tracking new legislation that could slap one hundred percent tariffs on Indian imports due to the country's continued purchase of Russian oil. If passed, everyday products imported from India could become far more expensive in North America as global sanctions pressure international trade relationships.

Switching to technology, U.S. officials are weighing strict security controls on artificial intelligence following a series of recent hacking incidents at OpenAI. This means public AI software tools could soon face much tighter user access rules, as governments shift away from light oversight toward active regulation.

In a related step, the U.S. government has banned imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots, robotic dogs, and solar inverters over national security risks. These restrictions mean solar equipment and advanced robotics may become significantly costlier for consumers as technology supply chains break apart along geopolitical lines.

Next, global food authorities are issuing a stark warning, urging agriculture sectors around the world to prepare for an era of extreme weather. As severe heatwaves and unpredictable storms reduce crop harvests globally, everyday grocery bills are likely to keep rising.

Over in central Africa, a worsening Ebola outbreak is deepening severe food shortages across eastern Congo. Families in the region are facing acute risks of starvation as overlapping disease and food crises compound an already devastating humanitarian disaster.

In business, Microsoft shares jumped seven percent after the company announced massive new capital investments to build out its digital infrastructure and keep up with demand. For everyday users, this rapid expansion means cloud services and online tools should run faster and more reliably.

Meanwhile, Brazil has become the world’s top buyer of Chinese motor vehicles, with imports leaping by nearly one hundred and forty-seven percent. This shift means Brazilian buyers will likely gain broader access to cheaper electric vehicles, as Chinese carmakers aggressively expand into Latin America.

Turning to international news, Ukraine has found a new pressure point in Russia’s wartime economy by launching cyberattacks against its largest e-commerce platform. The disruption leaves Russian online shoppers facing severe delivery delays, highlighting how modern conflicts are increasingly targeting everyday digital networks.

Looking up, two impressive meteor showers are reaching their peak visibility this week, though a bright full moon might make them harder to spot. If you want to catch the show, try stepping outside away from city lights, as celestial events continue to offer a wonderful moment of wonder.

In legal news, Italy’s highest court has strengthened citizenship claims for foreign descendants of Italian emigrants. This ruling makes it much easier for people of Italian heritage around the world to secure a European Union passport and build closer ties with their ancestral homeland.

And finally, India’s spending on research and development has crossed zero point eight percent of its GDP for the first time in over a decade, driven by private companies. This boost in funding promises to open up exciting high-skilled research jobs as emerging economies pivot toward domestic innovation.

Before we sign off, here is a nice thought to leave you with today. We often think of prehistoric creatures living in the exact same ancient era, but Tyrannosaurus rex actually lived closer in time to modern humans than it did to Stegosaurus. By the time T-Rex roamed the Earth, Stegosaurus was already an ancient fossil beneath its feet.

That is your Sift Daily Briefing for today. Stay calm, stay informed, and have a wonderful day ahead.
